summary: Rise Health is a health-monitoring system for astronauts on long-duration missions, built for the "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts" challenge. It combines a wearable band, an Android app for each crew member and a web dashboard for the flight surgeon. The band streams heart rate, blood pressure and SpO2 over Bluetooth in real time; the app adds a daily reaction-time (psychomotor vigilance) test and a mood check-in, guided by "Rise", our mascot. Every signal is organized around NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight (Radiation, Isolation, Distance, Gravity, Environment) and turned into one simple answer: am I fit for the mission today, and what should I do next? Real space weather from NASA's DONKI service (solar flares, SEP events, geomagnetic storms) feeds the alerts. When a value goes out of range, Rise Health suggests an onboard action — move to the storm shelter, add a workout, postpone the EVA — so the crew can act even with a 20-minute communication delay to Earth. The flight surgeon sees a traffic light per astronaut, alerts, history, CSV reports and an open API with signed webhooks. The same approach can serve Antarctic bases, offshore platforms and remote communities.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Rise Health answers one question for every astronaut, every day: "Am I fit for the mission, and what should I do next?" It has three parts:

1. Wearable band (real hardware): a commercial BLE band streams heart rate, blood pressure and SpO2 to the phone in real time.

2. Crew app (Android): login by crew code, a morning routine guided by the mascot "Rise", Bluetooth band reading, a short Psychomotor Vigilance Test (reaction time, the kind of vigilance test NASA uses), a mood check-in, an alerts inbox with onboard actions, and a space-weather panel.

3. Mission dashboard (web): live view of the whole crew with a readiness traffic light (GO / CAUTION / NO-GO) per astronaut, crew detail with 24-hour history, alerts that can be acknowledged, 7-day reports with CSV export, user management, and an integration page (API keys + HMAC-signed webhooks) so other mission systems can consume or push data.

HOW IT WORKS

Every metric has a safe range and belongs to one of NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight (RIDGE: Radiation, Isolation & confinement, Distance from Earth, altered Gravity, hostile closed Environment), plus cardiovascular and immune pillars. When a value leaves its range, an alert is raised with a concrete onboard action (e.g. solar flare → move to the storm shelter; bone-density drop → resistive exercise; low vigilance → postpone the EVA). Space weather is real: the server polls NASA's DONKI API for solar flares, SEP events and geomagnetic storms. Metrics that a consumer device cannot measure (bone density, urinary calcium, radiation dose, etc.) are produced by a simulator and are always stored and displayed with a clear "SIM" label, ready to be replaced by real sensors. A simulated Mars-transit mission (3 simulated crew members + 1 real crew member wearing the band) runs continuously so the system always shows live data.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Autonomy: with up to 20 minutes of communication delay to Earth, the crew gets actionable guidance without waiting for ground control.

- Simplicity: dozens of signals become one readiness status and one next action.

- Interoperability: open REST API and webhooks; any new sensor or mission system can plug in.

- Benefits on Earth: the same system fits Antarctic stations, offshore platforms, remote towns and older adults living alone — wherever the doctor is far away.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLite, real-time simulator.

Dashboard: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, TanStack Query.

Mobile app: Capacitor 7 (Android), TypeScript, Chart.js, Bluetooth Low Energy plugin.

Data: NASA DONKI API (space weather).

Infrastructure: Google Cloud VM, Nginx, Let's Encrypt.

Presentation video: HyperFrames (HTML-to-video) and Kokoro TTS (AI narration voice).

CREATIVITY

A friendly mascot, inspired by the plush zero-gravity indicators flown on crewed missions, turns the daily health check into a routine rather than a medical exam. The whole system is organized with NASA's own human-research hazard framework, and it is honest by design: real and simulated data are always clearly separated.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Communication delay and crew autonomy; cognitive load (one answer instead of fifty numbers); data honesty (SIM labels); privacy and role-based access (crew codes, admin vs. flight surgeon); and extensibility to real medical devices in the future.

SI DISCLOSURE

Parts of the code and texts were developed with the assistance of Claude (Anthropic).
